1: Good morning, Mister President. Good morning, Professors. Thank you for the opportunity to present my work. I am Mouad Louhichi, and the thesis I am defending, supervised by Professor Mohamed Lazaar, is entitled: Cooperative Game Theory for Explainable AI in Recommendation Systems, A Shapley Framework for Actionable Insight. Keep one idea in mind: Shapley attribution is not just a way to explain a model after training. I show how it becomes one framework that explains black-box models, stays consistent across levels of detail, and guides how recommenders learn.
2: So here is the plan for the next forty minutes. I will start with the motivation and the concept of actionable insight, then the research context, the limitations and the research questions. Then the common experimental protocol, and the three contributions, each following the same path: the gap, the objectives, the methodology, the protocol, the results and the findings. I will close with the outcomes and the perspectives.
3: Let me start with the motivation. The first question is simple: why has explainability become a core requirement for modern recommenders?
4: Recommenders now decide what we see, watch and buy. They are accurate, but their reasoning is hard to understand. Three questions drive this thesis. First, scale: these models shape the experience of billions of users. Second, transparency: even state-of-the-art recommenders and clustering pipelines are often black boxes. Third, trust: can we build transparency into the model itself, instead of adding explanations later? And the thesis starts from one idea: accuracy and interpretability are two goals to achieve together, not competing objectives.
5: That brings me to the definition the thesis turns on. An explanation is actionable when it points to something we can actually change, and changing it clearly affects the output. It must be expressed in the language of the domain: acidity in wine, pollution in air quality, user preferences in recommenders. So a good explanation does not only describe what happened, it tells us what to change to improve the outcome.
6: Now the context. The history of this field is also the history of the interpretability problem. Early similarity-based approaches were easy to explain because they used visible features. Matrix factorization improved accuracy and scale, but hid the meaning in latent factors. Neural and graph models added power through hidden representations and message passing, and hypergraphs added richer relationships. At each step we gained predictive power while losing transparency. That growing gap is what this thesis addresses.
7: These are not only theoretical models. Netflix, Spotify, Amazon and Yelp already personalize the experience of millions of users. The performance is impressive, yet the user rarely knows why a specific item was selected. That is the situation this work starts from.
8: Now I will move from the motivation to the research problem. So, to see where the difficulty comes from, I will briefly review the main approaches and their limitations.
ap_content: The first family is content-based filtering. The principle is simple: the system recommends items according to their characteristics and the user's previous preferences. So it is naturally explainable, because the reason is a visible feature. But it needs rich metadata, and it tends to over-specialize on what the user already knows.
ap_cf: The second family is collaborative filtering. Here, the system does not use item features. Instead, it learns from the behaviour of similar users. And that can discover hidden patterns from interactions. But it suffers from the cold-start problem, because new users and new items have little history.
ap_hybrid: The third family combines hybrid approaches and matrix factorization. Matrix factorization is accurate and scalable, so it became very successful. But the learned user and item factors are latent, and their meaning is unknown. This is where the gap between accuracy and interpretability starts to grow.
ap_graph: The fourth family, and the most important for this thesis, is graph and hypergraph recommendation. These approaches represent users, items and interactions as connected structures, and through message passing they capture more complex relationships. Hypergraphs go further by joining a user, an item and a context in one relation. But the importance of each message remains hidden, so the model cannot explain which relationships actually mattered.
10: So this evolution leaves four limitations. The first is data sparsity: the interaction matrix is almost empty. The second is cold-start: new users and items have no history. The third is popularity bias: popular items get more exposure. And the one this thesis targets is the absence of interpretability. For clustering, it is even harder, because existing methods give either local or global explanations, but rarely both consistently.
11: These observations lead to three problems that shape this research. First, complex models are hard to explain in a way that is both faithful and actionable. Second, explanations often do not scale to large or multi-level data. And third, they are produced after training, so they describe the model without influencing how it learns. The central idea here is that Shapley attribution can address all three under one cooperative-game framework.
12: From this gap, five research questions follow. The first asks how Shapley values can explain black-box clustering faithfully, at both instance and cluster level. The second asks how this can extend to large-scale, multi-level clustering while staying consistent. The third moves beyond explanation and asks whether attribution can become part of how recommenders learn. The fourth asks whether this also improves ranking, context and diversity. And the fifth asks what we gain by reading both tasks through one cooperative-game view.
13: These questions lead to three contributions. The first introduces a Shapley framework for explaining black-box clustering, evaluated on Wine Quality. The second extends it to large-scale multi-level clustering on Beijing Air Quality, with a formal guarantee of consistency across levels. And the third, DyHuCoG, integrates cooperative attribution directly into hypergraph recommendation learning. Together they follow one progression: explain, scale, and finally act.
15: Before presenting the contributions, I will first describe the common experimental protocol used throughout the thesis. The objective is to make the evaluation consistent and reproducible across all experiments. I will present the datasets, the baselines, the evaluation metrics, and the computational environment.
ds_wine: Four datasets are used, covering both tasks: Wine Quality and Beijing Air Quality for clustering, MovieLens-1M and Amazon-Book for recommendation. The first dataset is the Portuguese White Wine Quality dataset. It contains 4,898 samples described by 11 physicochemical measurements, including acidity, density, sulphates, and alcohol. This dataset is particularly suitable for the first contribution because every variable has a clear meaning in the real domain. So when the explanation identifies an important factor, it can directly correspond to something a wine expert can understand and potentially influence.
ds_beijing: The second dataset is Beijing Multi-Site Air Quality. It contains 383,585 hourly observations collected from monitoring stations, including pollutant measurements and weather variables. Compared with wine data, this dataset introduces several additional challenges: much larger scale, environmental complexity, and temporal variation. This makes it an appropriate test case for evaluating whether explanations can remain meaningful in large multi-level structures.
ds_ml1m: For recommendation experiments, two datasets are considered. The first one is MovieLens-1M, containing approximately one million ratings from more than six thousand users over thousands of movies. It is a standard benchmark widely used in recommendation research, allowing comparison with existing methods.
ds_amazon: The second is Amazon-Book, which is much more sparse, with millions of interactions but a very low user-item density. This allows us to evaluate whether the proposed method remains effective when the available signal is limited.
18: Regarding the experimental design, reproducibility and prevention of data leakage are important considerations. For clustering experiments, cross-validation is used. For recommendation experiments, I use user-level time-ordered splits with validation-based early stopping. All experiments are repeated using multiple random seeds to ensure that the results are not dependent on a specific initialization.
19: The proposed approaches are compared with strong existing baselines. For clustering explanation, the main comparison is performed against LIME-based explanations, which represent one of the most common post-hoc explanation approaches. For recommendation, the comparison includes classical matrix factorization methods and recent graph and hypergraph recommenders, including HPCF.
metrics: Different evaluation metrics are used depending on the task. For recommendation, NDCG@20 is used as the main ranking metric. Also, coverage and intra-list diversity are evaluated because recommendation quality is not only about accuracy, but also about providing diverse and less biased results. For clustering, metrics such as Silhouette and Davies-Bouldin are used to evaluate the quality of the obtained partitions. These metrics allow us to evaluate both model performance and the quality of the explanations.
20: Finally, regarding the computational environment, clustering experiments were performed on a standard workstation, while recommendation experiments, especially DyHuCoG training, were performed using an RTX 4090 GPU. These configurations allow us to evaluate not only the performance of the proposed approaches, but also their practical computational requirements.
21: With this experimental framework established, I can now move to the first contribution of this thesis. The objective here is to answer the following question: can we explain the decisions of a black-box clustering model using a principled attribution method?
22: The difficulty comes from the nature of clustering itself. Unlike supervised learning, clustering does not have a predefined target variable. The model discovers groups directly from the data, which makes understanding the reason behind each cluster more challenging. Existing explanation approaches usually focus either on individual instances or on global cluster descriptions, but they rarely provide a unified explanation at both levels. So the first contribution investigates how Shapley attribution can provide a faithful explanation framework for black-box clustering.
23: This contribution has three main objectives. The first objective is to provide explanations at both cluster level and individual sample level. The second objective is to keep the explanations in the original feature space, because explanations are only useful when domain experts can understand them. The third objective is to rely on a theoretically grounded attribution method based on cooperative game theory.
dd_game: Before the methodology, let me introduce the mathematical foundation of this work: cooperative game theory. In a cooperative game, we have a set of players, possible coalitions between these players, and a value function that measures the contribution of each coalition. The main question is how to fairly distribute the total contribution among the different players. The Shapley value provides this solution by calculating the average marginal contribution of each player across all possible orders of participation. In this thesis, the players are the input features, and the Shapley value measures how much each feature contributes to the clustering result.
25: To apply Shapley values to clustering, the clustering problem is reformulated as a cooperative game. The players correspond to the features, and the value function represents the quality of the clustering obtained using a subset of features. In this work, the Silhouette score is used to measure this quality. But evaluating every possible feature coalition is computationally expensive. So a surrogate model is introduced to approximate the clustering decisions and make Shapley computation practical.
c1_protocol: The proposed pipeline contains four main steps. First, K-Means is applied to create the initial clusters. Second, a LightGBM classifier is trained to reproduce these cluster assignments. Third, TreeSHAP is applied to this surrogate model to compute feature contributions. Finally, the obtained explanations are compared with LIME. The key point is that the surrogate model must faithfully represent the original clustering behaviour.
27: One important choice concerns the number of clusters. From a purely geometric perspective, two clusters provide the best separation according to the clustering metrics. But three clusters are selected because they provide more meaningful chemical interpretations. This choice illustrates an important principle of this thesis: the goal is not only to optimize mathematical criteria, but also to obtain explanations that can support human understanding and decision-making.
28: The results show that several variables play a major role in explaining the wine clusters. The most important factors include density, pH, acidity, sulfur dioxide variables, and alcohol content. These variables are meaningful because they correspond to real physicochemical properties of wine. More importantly, the explanation is not limited to a global ranking. It also shows that different clusters are characterized by different combinations of important variables.
31: This allows us to answer the first research question. Shapley values can explain black-box clustering when the surrogate model provides sufficient fidelity. They provide both global and local explanations while keeping the attribution connected to the original features. Compared with approaches such as LIME, the main advantage is that Shapley values are based on a formal cooperative-game foundation with desirable properties such as fairness and consistency.
32: To summarize Contribution I, the main achievement is the introduction of a Shapley-based framework for explaining black-box clustering. The approach provides explanations at different levels while maintaining the meaning of the original variables. So the explanations are not only mathematically grounded, but also understandable from a domain perspective.
33: But this first contribution also presents some limitations. First, the quality of the explanation depends on the fidelity of the surrogate model. Second, the evaluation is performed on tabular data, so the generalization to other data types remains open. Finally, the explanation remains single-level. It explains one clustering structure, but does not explain how feature importance changes across different levels of organization. This limitation motivates the second contribution.
34: The main takeaway from Contribution I is that Shapley attribution provides a principled way to understand an unsupervised model. But real-world datasets are often much larger and may contain hierarchical structures. So the next question is whether the same explanation principle can remain meaningful when moving from one level of analysis to several levels.
35: This brings me to the second contribution of the thesis. The objective is to extend Shapley-based explanation from single-level clustering to large-scale and multi-level clustering. This contribution addresses the second research question.
36: The challenge in this case is not only scale, but also consistency across levels. When a large cluster is divided into smaller sub-clusters, the explanation should help us understand both the global structure and the specific characteristics of each sub-group. But existing approaches do not provide a formal relationship between the explanation of a parent cluster and the explanations of its children. This is the main research gap addressed in this contribution.
37: This contribution has three objectives. First, to design a multi-level explanation framework where each level has its own surrogate model. Second, to establish a formal relationship between explanations at different levels of the hierarchy. Third, to evaluate whether this framework remains practical and meaningful on a large environmental dataset.
38: The proposed approach follows a recursive strategy. First, the complete dataset is partitioned into coarse clusters. Then, each cluster can be further divided into smaller sub-clusters. At every level, a surrogate model is trained and SHAP values are computed using the same original feature space. This allows the importance of variables to be compared across different levels while preserving interpretability.
39: The main theoretical contribution of this work is Proposition 6.1. This proposition establishes a relationship between the explanation of a parent cluster and the explanations of its child clusters. The parent attribution can be expressed as a size-weighted combination of child attributions, plus a residual term. This residual mainly reflects the difference introduced by surrogate approximation. So changes in importance across levels are not considered inconsistencies, but rather structured variations that can be interpreted.
c2_protocol: The experimental protocol follows the same general principles as the first contribution. The Beijing Air Quality dataset is first clustered at a global level. Then, each cluster is further divided to create a multi-level structure. At each level, a dedicated surrogate model is trained and SHAP explanations are computed. Finally, the proposed relationship is evaluated through aggregation and sensitivity analysis.
40: The clustering results show that the obtained structure is meaningful. The selected solution achieves a Silhouette score of approximately 0.63 and a Davies-Bouldin score around 0.55. The stability analysis also shows that the conclusions remain consistent under changes in modelling parameters such as the number of clusters, projection dimension, and surrogate complexity.
41: The global explanation reveals an interesting environmental interpretation. The most important variables are temperature, dew point, and pressure, followed by pollutants such as carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide, and particulate matter. This shows that pollution patterns are not determined only by pollutant concentrations themselves. Weather conditions influence how pollutants accumulate, disperse, and interact.
43: When moving from the global level to individual clusters, the explanation changes. At the global level, variables such as temperature and dew point explain the main environmental regimes. But inside each regime, different variables become important. For example, one cluster may be characterized by warmer conditions and ozone-related behaviour, while another may correspond to winter pollution involving particulate matter and other pollutants. These differences are not contradictions. They provide a more detailed understanding of the data structure.
45: This allows us to answer the second research question. Shapley explanations can be extended to large-scale and multi-level clustering when the hierarchy is explicitly defined and the approximation process is transparent. The main remaining limitation is that attribution is still performed after the model has been created.
46: To summarize Contribution II, the main achievement is extending explainability from a single clustering level to a hierarchical and large-scale scenario. The explanation remains connected to the original variables while providing insight at different levels of detail.
47: But some limitations remain. The clustering process is still static, even though the air-quality data have a temporal dimension. The explanations continue to depend on surrogate models and approximation techniques. Most importantly, attribution is still post-hoc: it explains what the model has already learned, but it does not participate in the learning process itself. This observation leads naturally to the third contribution, where explanation becomes part of model optimization.
48: The main takeaway from Contribution II is that Shapley attribution stays consistent across levels of detail once the hierarchy is explicit. The explanation therefore becomes interpretable at scale. It still describes a partition that was computed in advance, which raises the question behind the third contribution: can attribution become part of the learning itself?
49: This brings me to the third contribution of this thesis: DyHuCoG, which stands for Dynamic Hypergraph Cooperative Game. This contribution represents the main transition of the thesis. In the first two contributions, Shapley values were used to explain models after they were trained. Here, the objective is different: can attribution become part of the learning process itself?
50: The main limitation of existing hypergraph recommendation models is that they usually treat the different relationships in the graph structure in a similar way. But in real recommendation scenarios, not every interaction contributes equally to the final prediction. Some user-item-context relationships are more informative than others. The idea behind DyHuCoG is therefore to use cooperative attribution during training, so that the model can learn which relationships provide the most valuable information.
51: This contribution addresses two main research questions. The first question is whether cooperative attribution can move beyond post-hoc explanation and become part of the recommendation learning process. The second question is whether this integration can improve recommendation quality while maintaining contextual relevance and diversity. To answer these questions, DyHuCoG combines hypergraph learning with Shapley-based attribution. The first objective is to model recommendation as a cooperative game involving users, items, and contextual information. The second objective is to introduce a preference-aware Monte Carlo Shapley estimation mechanism inside hypergraph message passing. The third objective is to optimize several objectives together: ranking accuracy, diversity, and contextual relevance. The main idea is that the same mechanism used to explain importance can also guide the learning process.
52: To formulate this idea, recommendation is represented as a cooperative game. The players are the different elements involved in the recommendation process: users, items, and contextual information. Their interactions are represented through hyperedges, which allow modelling higher-order relationships. The contribution of each element is estimated through Shapley values. So instead of learning only from the existence of a relationship, the model also considers the contribution of this relationship to the final objective.
54: The main challenge is that exact Shapley computation is computationally impossible for large recommenders. The number of possible coalitions grows exponentially with the number of players. So DyHuCoG uses Monte Carlo approximation. Instead of evaluating all possible coalitions, we sample a limited number of permutations and estimate the average marginal contribution. This provides a practical approximation while preserving the main properties of Shapley attribution.
55: This slide presents the architecture of DyHuCoG. The model starts from a hypergraph recommendation structure where information is propagated through message passing. The main modification is the introduction of Shapley-based weights inside this propagation process. Important relationships receive stronger influence, while less informative relationships contribute less. An attention mechanism is also introduced to stabilize the learning process. Finally, the objective function combines ranking optimization, diversity, contextual information, and regularization.
c3_protocol: The evaluation is performed on two recommendation benchmarks: MovieLens-1M and Amazon-Book. The proposed method is compared with several baseline approaches, including recent graph and hypergraph recommenders. The evaluation considers ranking quality using NDCG and Recall, but also evaluates coverage and diversity. This is important because a recommendation system should not only be accurate, but should also provide varied and meaningful recommendations.
57: The results on MovieLens-1M show that DyHuCoG achieves the best performance among the evaluated methods. Compared with the strongest baseline, HPCF, the NDCG score improves from 0.2528 to 0.2775, representing an improvement of approximately 9.8 percent. Recall also improves, while coverage and diversity remain higher. This shows that the proposed approach does not improve accuracy by simply recommending the most popular items, but also maintains recommendation variety.
58: The same evaluation is conducted on Amazon-Book, which represents a much more challenging sparse recommendation scenario. Despite the higher difficulty, DyHuCoG continues to outperform the baselines. The improvement compared with HPCF reaches approximately 13.3 percent in NDCG. This result is important because it shows that cooperative attribution remains useful even when the available interaction information is limited.
60: To understand the contribution of each component, an ablation study is performed. The results show that each component plays an important role. Removing contextual information produces a significant degradation, which confirms the importance of context-aware recommendation. Removing Shapley weighting also reduces performance, demonstrating that cooperative attribution contributes directly to the learning process. So the improvement comes from the combination of hypergraph modelling, context information, and cooperative attribution.
61: Of course, integrating Shapley estimation into training introduces an additional computational cost. DyHuCoG requires more training time than traditional hypergraph recommenders because attribution is computed during learning. But inference remains practical, with recommendation latency at a reasonable level. So the additional computational complexity is a trade-off for obtaining a more accurate and interpretable model.
62: To verify that the improvements are not due to random variation, statistical validation is also performed. The comparison is conducted using user-level recommendation results. The statistical tests confirm that the improvements over the baseline are significant. The effect size also shows that the improvement is not only statistically detectable, but also practically meaningful.
64: These results allow us to answer the third and fourth research questions. For the third question, the answer is yes: Shapley attribution can move beyond post-hoc explanation and become part of the learning process. For the fourth question, the answer is also yes: DyHuCoG improves recommendation quality while maintaining diversity and contextual relevance. So attribution becomes not only an explanation mechanism, but also a learning mechanism.
65: To summarize Contribution III, DyHuCoG transforms the role of explanation. Instead of generating explanations after training, the model uses attribution information while learning. This creates a direct connection between what the model optimizes and what the explanation reveals.
66: But this contribution also has limitations. First, the integration of Shapley estimation increases computational cost. Second, the effectiveness of the approach depends on the availability of meaningful contextual information. Third, Monte Carlo estimation can still be improved through more advanced sampling strategies. Finally, the current evaluation is offline, and a future direction is to evaluate how users perceive and benefit from these explanations.
67: The main message of DyHuCoG is that attribution can become a first-class component of artificial intelligence models. Explanation is no longer only an observation after the model is built. It becomes part of the methodology used to train the model itself.
68: I will now summarize the main outcomes of this thesis and present the future perspectives. The objective is to connect the three contributions and highlight the common idea that links them together.
69: The three contributions follow a common progression: explain, scale, and guide. The first contribution explains black-box clustering using Shapley attribution and meaningful domain variables. The second contribution extends this idea to large-scale and multi-level structures while maintaining consistency between explanations. The third contribution moves beyond explanation and uses attribution to guide the learning process of recommenders. Together, these contributions show how cooperative game theory can provide a unified perspective for explainable AI.
70: This research has resulted in three journal publications as first author. These publications correspond to the three main stages of the thesis: explainable clustering, multi-level explainability, and cooperative recommendation learning. They reflect the progressive development of the proposed framework.
71: Several limitations remain open after this work. First, exact Shapley computation remains expensive, requiring approximation methods. Second, surrogate-based explanations depend on the quality of the approximation. Third, the current experiments are mainly offline and based on benchmark datasets. Finally, actionability should be evaluated more directly with human users to measure whether explanations actually improve understanding and decision-making.
72: These limitations naturally define several future research directions. The first direction is improving Shapley estimation through more efficient and adaptive sampling strategies. The second direction is extending the framework to dynamic and online recommenders where preferences evolve over time. The third direction is conducting user-centered evaluations to measure trust and usefulness. Finally, the framework could be extended toward other trustworthy AI objectives such as fairness.
73: To conclude, this thesis shows that cooperative game theory gives one common framework for explainable AI across clustering and recommendation. The main contributions demonstrate four important points. First, Shapley attribution provides a principled way to measure contribution. Second, it can explain black-box clustering using meaningful variables. Third, it can remain interpretable when moving to large-scale and multi-level structures. Finally, it can become part of the learning process itself through DyHuCoG. The main message is that explanation need not stay a description of what happened. It can become a way to understand, control and improve AI systems.
